newsitem.title: LATVIA: Balts wary of secret NATO deal at Helsinki summit.
newsitem.headline: Balts wary of secret NATO deal at Helsinki summit.

text.p: The Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia fear Russia and the U.S. may sell them out in a secret deal over NATO expansion, according to diplomats here.
President Bill Clinton's main aim at next week's Helsinki summit is to persuade Boris Yeltsin to accept NATO enlargement and convince him that it poses no threat to Russia.

But some Baltic officials are worried that Clinton may accept a deal with Yeltsin whereby Moscow removes its objections to former Warsaw Pact allies Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary entering NATO in return for a promise that the Balts will never be accepted into the alliance.
"Our worst concern is that there will be a sellout of the Balts," said one diplomat.
Russia has been furious at Baltic attempts to get into NATO, regarding it as a serious threat to its security to have such close neighbours as members of its Cold War foe.
The Baltic states were some of the most heavily militarised of the Soviet republics during the 50 years they were unwilling members of the Soviet Union.
Latvia and Estonia also have large ethnic Russian minortities -- around 30 percent in both cases, while in Lithuania Russians make up some eight percent of the population.
Moscow saw the three small nations as its Western bulwark and the coast bristled with navy and submarine bases.

But diplomats said they were hopeful that Clinton would not buckle under to any Russian demands for the Balts to be refused admittance to NATO, saying this would go against previously-stated U.S. policy.
"The idea is in the air that there may be a sellout but we think that at the end of the 20th century any sellouts are hardly possible," said one Latvian diplomat.
"The mood here is that it is not likely that the U.S. will make any implicit promises not to admit the Baltics," the diplomat added.
Although the Balts realise that early membership of NATO is impossible, they still believe the door remains open and want Clinton to make a public statement on this in Helsinki.

Funds for the three countries are tight as they reform their economies but they want to modernise and re-equip their armed forces to defend themselves and come to the armed assistance of other NATO members, a key condition for NATO membership.
Apart from Russian objections, the Balts' inability to defend other NATO states has been cited as one of the main reasons NATO is unwilling to accept them now.
Baltic diplomats said they would be pleased with a clear and public statement by Clinton that entry for Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia into the alliance was not a question of 'if' but of 'when.'
They also said they would like to see a statement from Yeltsin, saying Russia would respect the rights of the Balts to seek their own security path without inteference.
The three small nations of around eight million people have been plagued during their history by the deals of more powerful neighbours, deciding their fate without their knowledge.
The notorious Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact of 1939, under which Nazi Germany and Stalin divided the Balts between them, is still a bitter memory for all Balts.
It still colours their attitudes to any meetings between powerful nations where questions about the three nations are likely to be on the agenda.
